title: Contemporary Global Governance & Structures of the Global Economy
subject: The Contemporary World
description: Global governance vs. world government, state & non-state actors, treaties vs. soft law, governance theories, pillars of the global economy, outsourcing, surpluses/deficits, GVCs, and market integration.

questions.question: What is the key distinction between 'global governance' and a 'world government'?
options: Global governance is a single centralized world parliament that taxes every citizen.
There is no central world government; global governance coordinates states, IGOs, and non-state actors through voluntary cooperation, negotiation, and agreements.
Global governance bans sovereign states from making domestic laws.
World government currently runs all local city halls.
questions.answer: There is no central world government; global governance coordinates states, IGOs, and non-state actors through voluntary cooperation, negotiation, and agreements.
questions.explanation: Global governance relies on shared rules, norms, and institutions rather than a supreme global authority.

questions.question: In global governance, how do Sovereign States, IGOs, and Non-State Actors differ?
options: Sovereign States hold legal/treaty authority; IGOs (UN, WTO, ASEAN) are intergovernmental bodies setting/monitoring standards; Non-State Actors (NGOs, MNCs, media) advocate, invest, and shape agendas.
NGOs are the only bodies allowed to sign treaties.
MNCs hold seats as sovereign voting countries in the UN General Assembly.
IGOs have no member governments.
questions.answer: Sovereign States hold legal/treaty authority; IGOs (UN, WTO, ASEAN) are intergovernmental bodies setting/monitoring standards; Non-State Actors (NGOs, MNCs, media) advocate, invest, and shape agendas.
questions.explanation: Effective governance coordinates sovereign states alongside global/regional IGOs and civil/private non-state actors.

questions.question: What distinguishes 'international treaties/conventions' from 'soft law' in global cooperation?
options: Treaties (e.g., Paris Agreement) are legally binding with reporting standards; soft law consists of non-binding norms and voluntary standards.
Soft law carries automatic military penalties; treaties are purely optional suggestions.
Treaties only apply to private companies; soft law applies only to kings.
Both are legally identical.
questions.answer: Treaties (e.g., Paris Agreement) are legally binding with reporting standards; soft law consists of non-binding norms and voluntary standards.
questions.explanation: Alongside treaties and soft law, Public-Private Partnerships unite governments, businesses, and civil society.

questions.question: In global governance, what is the 'free-rider problem'?
options: Tourists riding buses without paying local fares
Certain states enjoying the benefits of global public goods (like climate stability or security) without contributing their fair share
Unequal voting rights in the UN Security Council
Too many treaties covering the same river
questions.answer: Certain states enjoying the benefits of global public goods (like climate stability or security) without contributing their fair share
questions.explanation: The free-rider problem, uneven compliance/enforcement, and institutional fragmentation are key obstacles to cooperation.

questions.question: What is 'institutional fragmentation' in global governance?
options: Building physical walls around embassies
Overlapping jurisdictions and conflicting mandates among different international institutions
Translating treaties into multiple languages
Holding UN summits in different cities
questions.answer: Overlapping jurisdictions and conflicting mandates among different international institutions
questions.explanation: Fragmentation complicates coordination alongside sovereignty tensions and unequal power between wealthy and developing states.

questions.question: While no nation can opt out of globalization entirely, what policy choices do national governments still retain?
options: Choosing their level of openness toward trade, capital investment, visitors, immigrants, refugees, and internet traffic
Deciding whether gravity applies within their borders
Preventing climate change from crossing their airspace
Abolishing all neighboring countries
questions.answer: Choosing their level of openness toward trade, capital investment, visitors, immigrants, refugees, and internet traffic
questions.explanation: States navigate globalization by calibrating openness and domestic safeguards.

questions.question: Match the global governance theory to its core view: Realism vs. Liberal Institutionalism.
options: Realism: states act under international anarchy driven by national interest and relative power; Liberal Institutionalism: international institutions reduce uncertainty, lower transaction costs, and foster cooperation.
Realism: institutions eliminate power politics; Liberal Institutionalism: cooperation is impossible.
Realism: values/norms drive everything; Liberal Institutionalism: only MNCs matter.
Realism: focuses solely on Global South marginalization; Liberal Institutionalism: rejects all treaties.
questions.answer: Realism: states act under international anarchy driven by national interest and relative power; Liberal Institutionalism: international institutions reduce uncertainty, lower transaction costs, and foster cooperation.
questions.explanation: Compare Realism's power-centric skepticism with Liberal Institutionalism's emphasis on cooperative rules.

questions.question: Which three theoretical perspectives examine (1) shared norms/values reshaping state interests, (2) historical Western dominance marginalizing the Global South, and (3) collective management of climate/health stability?
options: (1) Constructivism, (2) Critical & Postcolonial, (3) Global Public Goods
(1) Realism, (2) Mercantilism, (3) Protectionism
(1) Behavioralism, (2) Monetarism, (3) Isolationism
(1) Structuralism, (2) Hedonism, (3) Feudalism
questions.answer: (1) Constructivism, (2) Critical & Postcolonial, (3) Global Public Goods
questions.explanation: Table 6 outlines five perspectives: Realism, Liberal Institutionalism, Constructivism, Critical & Postcolonial, and Global Public Goods.

questions.question: Which four requirements are necessary for effective global policy according to Part 7 §8?
options: Collective management, fair representation (including developing nations), accountability & transparency, and inclusiveness (state + private + civil society)
Secrecy, unilateral veto power, trade embargoes, and closed borders
Exclusive control by MNCs without public oversight
Eliminating all NGOs and local governments
questions.answer: Collective management, fair representation (including developing nations), accountability & transparency, and inclusiveness (state + private + civil society)
questions.explanation: Synchronized action and fair representation build legitimacy and prevent weak links.

questions.question: How is the 'Global Economy' defined, and what are its five pillars?
options: All national economies combined into one interconnected system; Pillars: International Trade (visible/invisible), Finance & Capital Flows (FDI/FX), Global Production Networks, MNCs, and Cross-Border Labor Mobility
Only gold reserves held in Europe; Pillars: Tariffs, Quotas, Embargoes, Barter, and Guilds
A single currency controlled by the UN; Pillars: Local farms only
Strictly domestic retail stores
questions.answer: All national economies combined into one interconnected system; Pillars: International Trade (visible/invisible), Finance & Capital Flows (FDI/FX), Global Production Networks, MNCs, and Cross-Border Labor Mobility
questions.explanation: Operating on global supply and demand, disruptions in one region directly affect prices and jobs worldwide.

questions.question: In international trade terminology, what is the difference between 'visible trade' and 'invisible trade'?
options: Visible trade exchanges physical goods; invisible trade exchanges services (e.g., BPO support, tourism, finance)
Visible trade happens during daytime; invisible trade happens at night
Visible trade uses paper money; invisible trade uses gold coins
Visible trade is legal; invisible trade is smuggling
questions.answer: Visible trade exchanges physical goods; invisible trade exchanges services (e.g., BPO support, tourism, finance)
questions.explanation: Both goods and cross-border services form core components of international trade.

questions.question: What historical examples in Part 8 show that outsourcing existed long before modern call centers?
options: Ancient Rome delegating tax collection to private agents, and early American industry outsourcing wagon cover production to Scotland using Indian raw materials
Gutenberg outsourcing the printing press to Mars
Ancient Egypt outsourcing pyramid building to software firms
Sumerians outsourcing cuneiform to CERN
questions.answer: Ancient Rome delegating tax collection to private agents, and early American industry outsourcing wagon cover production to Scotland using Indian raw materials
questions.explanation: Outsourcing—contracting external organizations for tasks previously handled internally—has deep historical roots.

questions.question: Match the three modern strategic types of outsourcing—ITO, BPO, and Transformational Outsourcing:
options: ITO: IT infrastructure/software dev; BPO: back-office/customer operations (call centers, accounting); Transformational: partnering for strategic innovation and structural change
ITO: farming tools; BPO: cargo shipping; Transformational: mining coal
ITO: import tariffs; BPO: border patrols; Transformational: currency printing
ITO: television ads; BPO: film directing; Transformational: book binding
questions.answer: ITO: IT infrastructure/software dev; BPO: back-office/customer operations (call centers, accounting); Transformational: partnering for strategic innovation and structural change
questions.explanation: Modern outsourcing spans technical IT (ITO), operational processes (BPO), and strategic transformation.

questions.question: Match the four surplus types in Table 7: Budget, Trade, Inventory, and Consumer Surplus.
options: Budget: tax revenues > spending; Trade: exports > imports; Inventory: supply > market demand; Consumer: max willingness to pay − actual price paid
Budget: imports > exports; Trade: spending > tax; Inventory: demand > supply; Consumer: price paid − production cost
All four measure government debt
All four measure foreign currency outflows
questions.answer: Budget: tax revenues > spending; Trade: exports > imports; Inventory: supply > market demand; Consumer: max willingness to pay − actual price paid
questions.explanation: For example, if you are willing to pay $100 and pay $70, your consumer surplus is $30.

questions.question: How do a Trade Deficit, Balance of Payments Deficit, and Fiscal Deficit differ?
options: Trade Deficit: imports > exports; BoP Deficit: foreign currency outflows > inflows (pressuring reserves); Fiscal Deficit: comprehensive gap including budget shortfall + total net state borrowing needs
Trade Deficit: exports > imports; BoP Deficit: tax revenue > spending; Fiscal Deficit: consumer savings
All three mean a country has extra unsold inventory
They are three words for consumer surplus
questions.answer: Trade Deficit: imports > exports; BoP Deficit: foreign currency outflows > inflows (pressuring reserves); Fiscal Deficit: comprehensive gap including budget shortfall + total net state borrowing needs
questions.explanation: Tables 7 and 8 carefully distinguish fiscal/budget balances from external trade and currency balances.

questions.question: What analytical trade-off can a persistent trade surplus vs. a persistent trade deficit signal?
options: Persistent surpluses can signal domestic underconsumption/imbalances; persistent deficits allow diverse goods access but heighten vulnerability to foreign shocks and currency swings
Surpluses always guarantee zero poverty; deficits automatically double exports
Surpluses weaken foreign reserves; deficits eliminate debt
Neither affects currency or domestic consumers
questions.answer: Persistent surpluses can signal domestic underconsumption/imbalances; persistent deficits allow diverse goods access but heighten vulnerability to foreign shocks and currency swings
questions.explanation: Economists evaluate both surpluses and deficits for their structural trade-offs rather than treating either simplistically.

questions.question: In a Global Value Chain (such as smartphone production across the US/South Korea, Taiwan, Japan, China, and Vietnam), where is the highest profit/value typically captured?
options: In basic physical assembly alone
In design, R&D, technological innovation, and branding/marketing rather than basic physical assembly
Only in raw iron ore mining
Strictly in local retail packaging
questions.answer: In design, R&D, technological innovation, and branding/marketing rather than basic physical assembly
questions.explanation: Higher value capture concentrates in R&D, IP, and high-tech design, while developing nations often handle assembly.

questions.question: What is the sequence of primary activities in Porter's Value Chain Model cited under GVC drivers?
options: Inbound logistics -> Operations -> Outbound logistics -> Marketing & Sales -> Service
Service -> Marketing -> Inbound logistics -> Mining -> Taxes
Tariffs -> Quotas -> Assembly -> Disposal
Imports -> Deficits -> Surpluses -> Liquidation
questions.answer: Inbound logistics -> Operations -> Outbound logistics -> Marketing & Sales -> Service
questions.explanation: Global Value Chains fragment Porter's value chain stages across optimal countries worldwide.

questions.question: According to WTO data cited in Part 8 §5, roughly how much of developing countries' exports are tied to GVCs, and what determines their gains?
options: Over half of developing country exports; gains depend heavily on domestic infrastructure and leave economies exposed to external supply shocks
Less than 1%; gains are guaranteed regardless of infrastructure
100%; developing nations face zero supply shock risk
Zero exports involve GVCs
questions.answer: Over half of developing country exports; gains depend heavily on domestic infrastructure and leave economies exposed to external supply shocks
questions.explanation: Stronger domestic infrastructure, skills, and upgrading help developing countries capture greater GVC value.

questions.question: Match the four types of Market Integration: Price, Financial, Trade, and Labor integration.
options: Price: commodity prices align across regions; Financial: linked stock/capital markets; Trade: FTAs/lowered tariffs (EU, USMCA, ASEAN); Labor: free cross-border worker mobility
Price: fixed government price ceilings; Financial: banning foreign banks; Trade: raising tariffs; Labor: closing visas
All four refer strictly to agricultural subsidies
All four apply only to domestic city markets
questions.answer: Price: commodity prices align across regions; Financial: linked stock/capital markets; Trade: FTAs/lowered tariffs (EU, USMCA, ASEAN); Labor: free cross-border worker mobility
questions.explanation: For example, EU citizens working in any EU member state without special visas illustrates Labor Market Integration.

questions.question: In Table 9 comparing Integrated Markets vs. Separate National Markets, what trade-off does an Integrated Market accept?
options: Wider market access and global competition in exchange for reduced national policy flexibility and higher exposure to international shocks
Complete policy autonomy with zero exposure to foreign shocks
High protectionist tariffs and strictly domestic competition
Zero foreign trade
questions.answer: Wider market access and global competition in exchange for reduced national policy flexibility and higher exposure to international shocks
questions.explanation: Separate markets retain independent national policymaking but face limited market access and domestic-crisis vulnerability.

questions.question: In Part 9's summary matrix, what key vulnerability pairs with the Cultural Realm benefit of cross-cultural learning and media sharing?
options: Threat of cultural homogenization and loss of local languages or traditions
Higher consumer product variety
Exchange rate volatility
Global supply chain bottlenecks
questions.answer: Threat of cultural homogenization and loss of local languages or traditions
questions.explanation: Every domain—Consumers, Business, Socio-Economic, Cultural, and Environmental—carries paired opportunities and risks.

questions.question: In the Environmental domain of Part 9, what contradiction exists between globalization's opportunity and vulnerability?
options: Opportunity: international agreements on biodiversity and sustainability; Vulnerability: higher carbon footprint from global shipping and rapid resource consumption
Opportunity: higher carbon emissions; Vulnerability: too many environmental treaties
Opportunity: zero shipping; Vulnerability: lack of imports
There are no environmental impacts from global trade
questions.answer: Opportunity: international agreements on biodiversity and sustainability; Vulnerability: higher carbon footprint from global shipping and rapid resource consumption
questions.explanation: Global trade enables environmental treaties yet simultaneously expands transport emissions and extraction.

questions.question: What does 'sovereignty tension' mean in contemporary global governance?
options: The persistent conflict between maintaining national autonomy and adhering to binding international governance commitments
Disagreements over soccer referee calls
Competition between smartphone operating systems
Conflicts strictly between neighboring cities
questions.answer: The persistent conflict between maintaining national autonomy and adhering to binding international governance commitments
questions.explanation: States want collective solutions to global problems while resisting limits on domestic authority.

questions.question: Which grouping correctly separates Global IGOs from Regional IGOs?
options: Global: UN, WTO, World Bank, IMF, WHO; Regional: EU, ASEAN
Global: ASEAN, EU; Regional: UN, WHO
Global: McDonald's, Apple; Regional: Red Cross
Global: Local city councils; Regional: WTO
questions.answer: Global: UN, WTO, World Bank, IMF, WHO; Regional: EU, ASEAN
questions.explanation: Global IGOs coordinate worldwide standards, whereas regional IGOs focus on economic integration and security within a region.

questions.question: When a major wheat drought and price surge in the United States directly pushes up bread prices in Europe and Africa, this demonstrates:
options: Price integration across global commodity markets
Labor market integration
Soft law
Inventory surplus
questions.answer: Price integration across global commodity markets
questions.explanation: Linked supply and demand cause regional commodity prices to align globally (adjusted for shipping/tariffs).

questions.question: When a sharp Wall Street stock drop immediately triggers sell-offs across Asian and European exchanges, this illustrates:
options: Financial market integration
Budget surplus
Free-rider problem
Cultural glocalization
questions.answer: Financial market integration
questions.explanation: Integrated capital markets transmit financial shocks across continents almost instantaneously.

questions.question: If a government collects $500B in annual taxes and spends $650B, what specific type of deficit occurs?
options: Budget deficit ($150B)
Trade surplus ($150B)
Inventory surplus
Consumer surplus
questions.answer: Budget deficit ($150B)
questions.explanation: A budget deficit occurs when government expenditure exceeds tax revenue in a fiscal year; trade deficit compares exports vs. imports.

questions.question: If Country X exports $200B in goods and imports $150B, Country X is experiencing a:
options: Trade surplus of $50B
Trade deficit of $50B
Budget deficit of $50B
Inventory deficit
questions.answer: Trade surplus of $50B
questions.explanation: Exports ($200B) minus Imports ($150B) = +$50B trade surplus.

questions.question: Within Non-State Actors in global governance, what primary roles do NGOs vs. MNCs play?
options: NGOs advocate for human rights, environment, and social justice; MNCs influence global trade flows, capital allocation, and technical standards
NGOs set global tariffs; MNCs write national constitutions
Neither NGOs nor MNCs interact with governments
Both are organs of the UN Security Council
questions.answer: NGOs advocate for human rights, environment, and social justice; MNCs influence global trade flows, capital allocation, and technical standards
questions.explanation: Non-state actors complement—and sometimes challenge—state authority in shaping global outcomes.

questions.question: What are 'Public-Private Partnerships' (PPPs) as a mechanism of international cooperation?
options: Multi-stakeholder collaborations uniting governments, businesses, and civil society to tackle shared problems
Secret treaties between two rival armies
Selling public schools to foreign banks
Bans on corporate research
questions.answer: Multi-stakeholder collaborations uniting governments, businesses, and civil society to tackle shared problems
questions.explanation: PPPs combine public legitimacy/regulation with private capital, innovation, and NGO outreach.

questions.question: Under the International Finance & Capital Flows pillar of the global economy, what does FDI stand for?
options: Foreign Direct Investment
Federal Domestic Income
Fixed Deficit Index
Fiscal Debt Integration
questions.answer: Foreign Direct Investment
questions.explanation: FDI, cross-border stock/bond markets, and foreign exchange trading drive international capital flows.
